prompt: What does a write send back to the server, in optimistic concurrency?

choices.text: A lock it took on the row before editing
choices.why: Nothing is locked; an offline phone would hold the lock for an hour.

choices.text: The time on the device's clock when it was made
choices.why: That is lesson 13's stamp, and it cannot say what the writer had seen.

choices.text: The version number it read
choices.why: Right. If the server's number has moved on, somebody wrote first.

choices.text: A hash of the whole planner
choices.why: One number per row is enough.

prompt: The phone sends s3 with version 1, and the server holds version 2. What does the lesson's server answer?

choices.text: 409, with the current row in the body
choices.why: Right. The phone learns version 2 exists and what it says.

choices.text: 404, because version 1 no longer exists
choices.why: The session exists; 404 is for a session that does not.

choices.text: 412, because no If-Match header was sent
choices.why: 412 is the If-Match spelling; this server checks a field in the body.

choices.text: 200, and it saves the phone's copy as version 3
choices.why: That would be last write wins again.

prompt: After a 409, the phone sends its own copy again, now with version 2. What happens to the tablet's tick?

choices.text: It survives as version 2 in the server's history
choices.why: The server keeps one row, not a history.

choices.text: The server refuses again, because version 2 was not the phone's
choices.why: The server checks only that the number matches, and it does.

choices.text: It survives, because the server merges the two
choices.why: The lesson's server merges nothing; the device has to.

choices.text: It is lost, as under last write wins
choices.why: Right. The version only made the loss take one more round trip.

prompt: Match each HTTP piece to what it does in a version check.

pairs.right: the version the server sends with a row
the version the client says it read
the answer when If-Match does not match
the lesson's answer to a stale version in the body

right_distractors: the answer when the row was deleted

prompt: What does a vector clock let two devices do that a version number does not?

choices.text: Resolve a conflict without asking anybody
choices.why: It only detects one; the lesson says so in bold.

choices.text: Detect a conflict with no single server counting
choices.why: Right. Each device keeps its own counter, and the row carries them all.

choices.text: Order writes by the real time they were made
choices.why: It reads no time at all.

choices.text: Store one integer per row
choices.why: That is the version number; a vector clock carries one per device.

choices.text: before
choices.why: The first is ahead on phone, so it is not before.

choices.text: concurrent
choices.why: Right. Each is ahead in one entry, so neither saw the other.

choices.text: after
choices.why: The second is ahead on tablet, so the first is not after.

choices.text: equal
choices.why: Equal clocks have the same value in every entry.

prompt: When a device receives another device's row, it merges the clocks by taking the ___ value of every entry.
Why does the lesson stay with version numbers for the planner?

choices.text: Vector clocks cannot tell an ordered write from a concurrent one
choices.why: That is exactly what they do; the run printed both.

choices.text: Vector clocks need every device's clock to be right
choices.why: They read no wall clock; a skewed phone gets the same answer.

choices.text: Node has no way to store a JSON object in SQLite
choices.why: A clock fits in a text column as JSON.

choices.text: It syncs through one server, so one integer per row is enough
choices.why: Right. Vector clocks are for when no single place sees every write first.

prompt: What is the base in a three-way merge?

choices.text: The version both devices started from
choices.why: Right. A field still at its base value was not touched by that side.

choices.text: The copy with the most fields changed
choices.why: The base is defined by history, not by a count.

choices.text: The server's current row
choices.why: That is theirs; the base is older.

choices.text: The first row ever written for that session, at version 1 forever
choices.why: The base moves: after a merge, the server's row becomes the new base.

prompt: Base minutes 20; the phone has 30; the server has 20. What does merge3 keep for minutes, and why?

choices.text: 20, because the server's value wins a tie
choices.why: There is no tie: the server never changed it.

choices.text: A conflict, since the two copies differ
choices.why: Two copies differing is not enough; both have to differ from the base.

choices.text: 30: only the phone moved it off the base
choices.why: Right. The server's 20 is the base value, untouched.

choices.text: 25, the average
choices.why: Nothing averages; the merge picks one side's value.

prompt: In the lesson's merge run, the second PUT was accepted. What version number did the server give the saved row?
A device keeps only its edited copy, not the row as the server last sent it. What can it no longer do on a 409?

choices.text: Tell which fields each side changed
choices.why: Right. Without the base, 30 against 20 does not say who moved it.

choices.text: Send anything with the server's version
choices.why: It can send; it just cannot know what it should send.

choices.text: Detect that a conflict happened at all
choices.why: The 409 itself says that.

choices.text: Read the server's current row from the reply
choices.why: The reply still carries it; that part does not depend on the device.

prompt: Which conflict does the lesson say to put in front of the person?

choices.text: Any concurrent edit of a session, so nothing is decided behind their back
choices.why: Different fields merge silently, and asking for them teaches people to tap through.

choices.text: A setting changed to two values
choices.why: For a setting, lesson 13's rule is right and nobody is asked.

choices.text: The same field of something they made, changed to two values
choices.why: Right. Only that case has no answer in the data.

choices.text: A field changed to the same value on both devices
choices.why: Both agree, so the merge keeps it.

prompt: What should the planner's conflict screen show? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: each value with the device and time it was made
choices.why: That is what lets the person recognise their own work.

choices.text: a way to type a third value
choices.why: Neither value may be the one they want.

choices.text: what is in conflict, in the person's words
choices.why: "Guitar, Wednesday: how long?" rather than a field name.

choices.text: the two version numbers the server compared
choices.why: Those are for the program; the person needs the values.

prompt: While one session waits for Ana to choose between 30 and 25 minutes, twenty other edits are in the outbox. What does the lesson say about them?

choices.text: They wait, so the planner does not sync around a dispute
choices.why: One session in dispute is no reason for twenty to wait.

choices.text: They sync; the conflict waits in its own table
choices.why: Right. A conflict must never block the outbox.

choices.text: They are merged into the disputed session
choices.why: They are edits of other rows.

choices.text: They are dropped until the conflict is resolved, then typed again
choices.why: Nothing is dropped anywhere in this lesson.

prompt: Put the phone's sync of lesson 13's morning in order, as sync.ts runs it.
items: merges base, its copy and the server's row

prompt: Two servers in different regions each accept writes to the same rows and exchange them every minute. Which tool from this lesson finds the conflicts?

choices.text: A version number checked by either server
choices.why: Each would count on its own, and two counters both reaching 2 say nothing.

choices.text: The server's clock, since both are kept right
choices.why: Right clocks still order by arrival; lesson 13 showed that loses an edit.

choices.text: merge3 alone, run when the rows arrive
choices.why: merge3 needs to know a conflict exists and what the base is; something else has to say so.

choices.text: A vector clock with an entry per server
choices.why: Right. No single place sees every write first, which is the case vector clocks are for.

prompt: Base done false; the phone has done true; the tablet has done true. What does merge3 do?

choices.text: Reports a conflict, because both sides changed it
choices.why: They changed it to the same value, so they agree.

choices.text: Keeps false, because the changes cancel out
choices.why: Two ticks do not cancel; both say done.

choices.text: Keeps true, as both agree
choices.why: Right. The first case of the rule: both agree, keep it.

choices.text: Asks the person which tick to keep
choices.why: There is nothing to choose between.
